concept.name: Bitmask Dynamic Programming

relationships.description: Connects Bitmask Dynamic Programming to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Compressing subsets of n <= 20 items into integer bitmasks to turn O(n!) permutations into O(n 2^n) or O(n^2 2^n) DP.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of bitmask DP—from Held-Karp TSP and canonical assignment to O(3^n) submask iteration and O(n 2^n) SOS DP.

spark.summary: Bitmask DP encodes a subset of n <= 20 elements as an integer 0 .. 2^n - 1, turning exponential factorial permutations (n!) into polynomial-in-subset DP (O(n^2 2^n) or O(n 2^n)).
spark.keyTakeaway: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set (n <= 20) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** When a problem's optimal substructure depends only on *which* subset $S$ of $n$ items has been used (and optionally the last item), all permutations of $S$ collapse into a single DP state.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Held-Karp TSP State Compression (0001 -> 0011 -> 0111 -> 1111) (MASK 0001 -> MASK 0011 -> MASK 1111); Choosing Bitmask DP Pattern by Input Bound n (n <= 20: O(n 2^n) -> n <= 18: O(n^2 2^n) -> n <= 15: O(3^n) -> SOS DP: O(n 2^n)); Selinger Bitmask Join-Order DP (Subsets of Relations) (Join Plan (1111) -> Left Subplan (0011) -> Right Subplan (1100) -> Base Scans).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Scale beyond $n = 20$ by exploiting linearity or splitting the set in half. Relational database query planners (PostgreSQL `geqo_threshold`, DuckDB) use **bitmask DP (Selinger / DPccp)** to pick the optimal join tree across $n$ tables!

**Failure Modes & Application:** Connect bitmask state compression to bitwise tricks, query planners, and graph algorithms.

learningJourney.title: What is Bitmask Dynamic Programming
learningJourney.explanation:
When a problem's optimal substructure depends only on *which* subset $S$ of $n$ items has been used (and optionally the last item), all permutations of $S$ collapse into a single DP state. **Bitmask DP** encodes $S \subseteq \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ as an $n$-bit integer `mask` where bit $i$ is `1` iff item $i \in S$.

Setting one unvisited bit (`mask | (1 << j)`) strictly increases the integer value of `mask`, giving a built-in topological DAG order over `0 .. (1 << n) - 1` and reducing $n!$ permutations to $O(n 2^n)$ or $O(n^2 2^n)$.

sectionDiagram.title: Held-Karp TSP State Compression (0001 -> 0011 -> 0111 -> 1111)
sectionDiagram.summary: Because setting a bit strictly increases mask, iterating mask from 0 to (1<<n)-1 processes states in valid topological order.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Bitmask Dynamic Programming works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Bitmask Compression (and complexity/memory traps)
learningJourney.explanation:
At $n = 18$, $18! \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15}$ is impossible, whereas $18^2 \cdot 2^{18} \approx 8.5 \times 10^7$ runs in under a second.

Watch three classic pitfalls:
1. **Accidental $O(4^n)$ Submask Loop**: Iterating `0..2^n-1` inside `0..2^n-1` takes $1.07 \times 10^9$ ops at $n=15$, whereas `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` takes $O(3^n) \approx 1.4 \times 10^7$.
2. **Redundant Dimension in Assignment**: When assigning item `i` to worker `k`, you only need `dp[mask]` (not `dp[i][mask]`) because `popcount(mask)` uniquely determines `i`!
3. **OOM on 2D `long` Tables**: `long[1 << 20][20]` uses 160 MB.

learningJourney.title: Where Bitmask DP is used
learningJourney.explanation: Use bitmask DP whenever $n \le 20$ and you need exact optimal solutions for routing, matching, or partitioning.

benefits: Guarantees global optimum for n <= 18 stops in milliseconds.
costs: Exponential memory O(n 2^n) makes n > 20 infeasible.

benefits: Handles arbitrary subset synergy costs that Hungarian algorithm cannot express.
costs: For linear 1-to-1 cost matrices with n > 20, use Hungarian O(n^3) or Min-Cost Max-Flow.

benefits: Switch to Meet-in-the-Middle (splits n=40 into two 2^20 halves), Branch-and-Bound, or ILP.
costs: 2^25 = 33M states already exceeds typical memory/time budgets.

learningJourney.explanation: Use iterative bottom-up loops over `mask` (avoiding Python recursion overhead) and `int.bit_count()` for assignment.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Bitmask DP vs. Meet-in-the-Middle vs. Hungarian
learningJourney.explanation: Scale beyond $n = 20$ by exploiting linearity or splitting the set in half.

benefits: Exact optimum for arbitrary subset-dependent costs up to n <= 20.
Solves subset-sum / partition problems up to n = 40 by merging two 2^(n/2) halves.
costs: Requires problem structure to be decomposable across two halves.

benefits: Polynomial O(n^3) for linear 1-to-1 assignment even at n = 1,000.

learningJourney.title: Production example: SQL Join-Order Optimizer (System R / Selinger DP)
learningJourney.explanation: Relational database query planners (PostgreSQL `geqo_threshold`, DuckDB) use **bitmask DP (Selinger / DPccp)** to pick the optimal join tree across $n$ tables! Each `mask` represents a subset of joined relations, and `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` enumerates candidate left/right subplans.

options.text: The number of set bits popcount(mask) uniquely determines which worker is currently being assigned
options.feedback: Correct: if workers 0..k-1 are assigned in order, k = mask.bit_count(), saving a factor of n in both time and memory.

options.text: Bitmasks automatically sort tasks by cost

options.feedback: A bitmask encodes the entire subset of assigned tasks.

_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
